newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says open for meeting with China at APEC.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says open for meeting with China at APEC.

text.p: Taiwan's delegate to the APEC summit said on Friday he would be open for talks with China's President Jiang Zemin at the gathering but that no such meeting had been scheduled.

"...Meeting with Mr Jiang Zemin is inevitable. A handshake and greeting are natural," Koo Chen-fu told reporters before departing for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit in the Philippines. APEC leaders meet on November 25.
"Since there is no plan...what we talk about when we meet will depend on fate," Koo added.

Koo, a wealthy businessman and head of a quasi-official body empowered to negotiate with China in the absence of official ties, will represent President Lee Teng-hui at the summit at Subic Bay, the Philippines.
Manila, under public pressure from China, has rejected Taiwan's request that President Lee or Vice-President Lien Chan be allowed to attend the summit.
China has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949 and endeavours to isolate Lee and his exiled Chinese Nationalist government.
Taiwan, which still bans official contacts with communist China, sits in APEC as a customs territory, not a sovereign.
Koo played down expectations of a meeting with Jiang, who aside from being China's president is head of the Communist Party whose troops defeated the Nationalist government.
"APEC is a multilateral meeting not a bilateral negotiation. I have nothing scheduled with Mr Jiang," said Koo, himself a ranking Nationalist Party member and presidential adviser.
Koo represented Lee at the 1995 APEC summit in Osaka, Japan, but exchanged nothing more than a tense handshake with Jiang.
Koo said that Taiwan's frustrated bid to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), rather than a resumption of long-stalled Taiwan-China talks, would be his focus at APEC.

Koo said he had scheduled bilateral meetings with leaders of the Philippines, Malaysia and Singapore to discuss Taiwan's bid to join the world trade body -- an issue which like most others in Taiwan is coloured by its rivalry with China.

Beijing does not oppose Taiwan's WTO membership as a customs territory, but has said China's own entry should come first. The United States, Europe, Japan and Canada have made China's entry conditional on further trade liberalisations.
Political fireworks between Taiwan and China erupted in June 1995 after President Lee made a private visit to the United States, which Beijing saw as a move to promote independence.

After Lee's U.S. visit, Beijing suspended semi-official talks with Koo's state-sanctioned Straits Exchange Foundation and launched a campaign of military intimidation, which peaked ahead of Taiwan's March 23 presidential election.
Taipei officially espouses reunification but does not accept terms offered by Beijing, insisting that China first adopt democratic reforms like those carried out in Taiwan.
